prompt:
A recursive selection sort scans for the minimum, swaps it into the next position, then recurses with one fewer item. Solve its running-time recurrence:

```formula
T(n) = T(n − 1) + n
where
T: the running time of the recursive selection sort on n items
n: the number of items still to sort
In words: One call removes a single item, with work proportional to the current size.
```

options.text: Θ(n log n), treating the single child as a Master Theorem case
options.explanation: The theorem needs a fixed fractional size reduction. This recurrence subtracts one item instead, so its assumptions fail.

Correct. Unrolling adds a decreasing arithmetic series.

```formula
T(n) = n + (n − 1) + … + 1
T(n) = n(n + 1)/2 = Θ(n^2)
T(0) = 0
where
T: the counted scan work on n items, with zero cost at size zero
n: the number of items still to sort
Θ: a tight growth bound up to fixed factors
…: "and so on" down to 1
In words: Unrolling adds a decreasing arithmetic series.
```
Each level does linear work, not constant, and there are n levels.

There is only one child per level. An exponential doubling pattern would require two children one item smaller.

```formula
T_other(n) = 2T_other(n − 1) + 1
where
T_other: the cost of that different branching recurrence
n: the number of items still to sort
In words: There is only one child per level. An exponential doubling pattern would require two children one item smaller.
```

workedExample:
The Master Theorem doesn't apply (the size shrinks by 1, not by a factor). Unroll:

```formula
T(n) = n + T(n − 1)
T(n) = n + (n − 1) + T(n − 2)
T(n) = n + (n − 1) + … + 1
T(n) = n × (n + 1) / 2
T(0) = 0
where
T(n): the counted scan work on n items, using zero cost at size zero for this exact sum
n: the number of items still to sort
…: "and so on" down to 1
In words: each call scans its whole remaining range and passes on a problem one smaller, so the scans add up to about half of n squared.
```

So **Θ(n^2)**, with quadratic growth. Rule of thumb: when the problem shrinks by a constant amount, there are about n levels, and you sum the per-level work.

prompt:
Which listed recurrences can be solved **directly** with the standard three-case Master Theorem? Select all that apply.

```formula
T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
where
T: the running time in basic steps
a: the fixed number of subproblems
b: the fixed shrink factor, greater than one
f: the outside-work function
n: the input size
In words: Equal-size recursive children are described by a fixed child count and shrink factor, plus outside work.
```

options.text: Eight half-size calls plus quadratic work
options.explanation:
Yes. Eight half-size calls give critical exponent three; quadratic outside work is polynomially smaller.

```formula
T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2
log_2(8) = 3
T(n) = Θ(n^3)
where
T: the running time in basic steps
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: Eight half-size calls give critical exponent three; quadratic outside work is polynomially smaller.
```

options.text: One call one item smaller, plus constant work
options.explanation:
No. Subtracting one is not fixed fractional splitting. Unrolling instead gives linear growth.

```formula
T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1
where
T: the running time in basic steps
n: the input size
In words: Subtracting one is not fixed fractional splitting. Unrolling instead gives linear growth.
```

No. The subproblems have different sizes, which the Master Theorem doesn't allow. Akra–Bazzi gives Θ(n log n).

```formula
T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n
where
T: the running time in basic steps
n: the input size
In words: The subproblems have different sizes, which the Master Theorem doesn't allow. Akra–Bazzi gives Θ(n log n).
```

Here n is the current subproblem size.

options.text: Three quarter-size calls plus linear-times-log work
options.explanation:
Yes. Linear-times-log outside work is polynomially above the subunit critical exponent, and the children’s outside work is at most three quarters of the parent’s.

```formula
T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log(n)
log_4(3) ≈ 0.79
3(n/4)log(n/4) ≤ (3/4)n log(n)
T(n) = Θ(n log(n))
where
T: the running time in basic steps
log: the base-two logarithm
log_4: the base-4 logarithm
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
≈: approximately equal
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Linear-times-log outside work is polynomially above the subunit critical exponent, and the children’s outside work is at most three quarters of the parent’s.
```

options.text: Two half-size calls plus linear divided by log work
options.explanation:
No. Outside work is smaller than linear only by a logarithm. It is neither polynomially smaller nor covered by the stated nonnegative-log-power balanced case. Akra–Bazzi gives the log-log result.

```formula
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log(n)
f(n) = n/log(n)
T(n) = Θ(n log(log(n)))
where
T: the running time in basic steps
f: the outside-work function
log: the base-two logarithm
n: the input size
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
In words: Outside work is smaller than linear only by a logarithm. It is neither polynomially smaller nor covered by the stated nonnegative-log-power balanced case. Akra–Bazzi gives the log-log result.
```

workedExample:
For each option, check equal-size fractional splitting, fixed parameters and the relevant growth case:

| Option | Form fits? | Case |
|---|---|---|
| First | yes | leaves: Θ(n^3) |
| Second | no | subtracts one |
| Third | no | unequal splits |
| Fourth | yes | root: Θ(n log n) |
| Fifth | yes | gap between cases |

The last one has the right form, but no case fits:

```formula
n / log(n) is not O(n^{1 − ε})
n / log(n) ≠ Θ(n × (log(n))^k),  k ≥ 0
where
n: the input size
log: the base-two logarithm
ε: epsilon, any fixed positive number
k: the power of log n allowed in case 2
O: Big-O, at most a constant times
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this rate up to constants
≠: is not equal to (here: does not have this growth rate)
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: n over log n is smaller than n, but only by a log factor, which is not enough for case 1 and the wrong direction for case 2.
```

**Polynomially smaller** requires a fixed positive-power gap, rather than only a logarithmic gap. The last card explicitly tests that failed condition.

prompt:
A student claims a linear bound for this recurrence using the argument below. What is wrong with the proof?

```formula
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ cn
T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2) + n = cn + n
cn + n = O(n)
where
O: an eventual upper growth bound up to a fixed factor
T: the running time
c: one fixed positive multiplier used in the induction
n: the positive item count
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: The last line is true for that expression, but does not show that the same guessed multiplier bounds the recurrence.
```

options.text: The inductive step increases the fixed multiplier instead of preserving it
options.explanation:
Correct. The last simplification silently uses a larger multiplier. Repeating that through the tree makes it grow with depth, exposing the hidden logarithm.

```formula
cn + n = (c + 1)n
where
c: the fixed constant in the guess, the same on both sides
n: the input size, a power of 2 of at least 2
In words: The last simplification silently uses a larger multiplier. Repeating that through the tree makes it grow with depth, exposing the hidden logarithm.
```

options.text: Nothing; the proof is valid but the Master Theorem is wrong here
options.explanation: The Master Theorem correctly gives Θ(n log n) (case 2). The proof is the thing that is broken. Here n is the current subproblem size.

options.text: The base case is missing, so the induction is incomplete
options.explanation: A base case is needed, but adding one wouldn't rescue this proof. The inductive step itself fails.

options.text: It should have divided by 2 instead of multiplying
options.explanation:
The multiplication is correct. The error is that the induction’s original fixed multiplier no longer bounds the resulting expression.

```formula
2c(n/2) = cn
where
c: the fixed constant in the guess, the same on both sides
n: the input size, a power of 2 of at least 2
In words: The multiplication is correct. The error is that the induction’s original fixed multiplier no longer bounds the resulting expression.
```

workedExample:
1. Induction must prove the **same fixed multiplier** that it assumes.
2. The attempted step adds another linear contribution, which cannot fit that same multiplier.
3. Hiding it inside Big-O silently increases the multiplier by one.
4. Repeating that increase through logarithmically many levels exposes the missing log factor.

```formula
T(n) ≤ cn + n
cn + n ≤ cn means n ≤ 0
c_new = c + 1
c_effective ≈ c + log_2(n)
where
T: the running time on input size n
c: the fixed constant in the guess, the same on both sides
c_effective: the multiplier after repeatedly accumulating those increases
c_new: the illegally increased multiplier
n: the input size, a power of 2 of at least 2
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(n/2) = log_2(n) − 1
≈: approximately equal
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: The attempted linear induction never closes with the same constant.
```

Use the linear-times-log guess instead:

```formula
T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2)log_2(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ cn log_2(n) − cn + n
T(n) ≤ cn log_2(n)   if c ≥ 1
where
T(n): the running time on input size n
n: a power-of-two input of at least four in this inductive step; the two-item base case is checked separately
c: the fixed constant in the guess, the same on both sides
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(n/2) = log_2(n) − 1
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: assuming the bound for size n/2 gives the same bound, with the same c, for size n.
```

That one closes, with the same c.

For the valid induction, begin at two items and choose the fixed multiplier to cover that base case. Handle one item separately because its logarithm is zero.
